title: Company
description: Employees, the departments they work in and who they report to.
schema: CREATE TABLE departments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, location TEXT NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, dept_id INTEGER REFERENCES departments(id), manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id), title TEXT NOT NULL, salary INTEGER NOT NULL, hire_date TEXT NOT NULL);

problems.title: High earners
problems.statement: List the `name` and `salary` of every employee who earns **more than 120000**, highest salary first.
problems.expected: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 120000 ORDER BY salary DESC
problems.hint: Filter with WHERE, then ORDER BY salary DESC.
problems.note: WHERE keeps the rows you want; ORDER BY only sorts what is left.

problems.title: Engineering team
problems.statement: Return the `name` of every employee who works in the **Engineering** department.
problems.expected: SELECT e.name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id WHERE d.name = 'Engineering'
problems.hint: Join employees to departments on dept_id = departments.id.
problems.note: An inner join drops employees without a department, which is what we want here.

problems.title: Departments with nobody
problems.statement: Which departments have **no employees**? Return the department `name`.
problems.expected: SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.id IS NULL
problems.hint: A LEFT JOIN keeps departments with no match; those rows have NULL employee columns.
problems.note: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL (an anti-join) and NOT EXISTS are the two usual ways. Avoid NOT IN when the column can be NULL.

problems.title: Average pay by department
problems.statement: For each department that has employees, return the department `name` and the average salary rounded to one decimal place (call it `avg_salary`).
problems.expected: SELECT d.name, ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 1) AS avg_salary FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name
problems.hint: Join, then GROUP BY the department.
problems.note: Every selected column is either grouped or aggregated.

problems.title: Big departments
problems.statement: Return the `name` and head count (`headcount`) of departments with **at least 3 employees**.
problems.expected: SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
problems.hint: A condition on COUNT(*) belongs in HAVING, not WHERE.
problems.note: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after.

problems.title: Above the department average
problems.statement: Return the `name` of employees who earn **more than the average salary of their own department**. Employees without a department are ignored.
problems.expected: SELECT e.name FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id)
problems.hint: A correlated subquery can average the salaries of the same dept_id as the current row.
problems.note: The subquery runs per row and refers to the outer row. A window function (AVG ... OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)) does the same in one pass.

problems.title: Top earner per department
problems.statement: For each department that has employees, return the department `name` (as `department`), the `name` of its best-paid employee (as `employee`) and that `salary`. Employees without a department are ignored.
problems.expected: SELECT department, employee, salary FROM (SELECT d.name AS department, e.name AS employee, e.salary AS salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d.id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS r FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id) WHERE r = 1
problems.hint: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC), then keep rank 1.
problems.note: Window functions cannot be filtered in the same SELECT, so wrap the ranking in a subquery or CTE.

problems.title: Salary ranking in Engineering
problems.statement: For employees in **Engineering**, return `name`, `salary` and `salary_rank`, where `salary_rank` is 1 for the highest salary, using no gaps between ranks. Order by rank.
problems.expected: SELECT e.name, e.salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS salary_rank FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id WHERE d.name = 'Engineering' ORDER BY salary_rank
problems.hint: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC). Filter to Engineering first.
problems.note: RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not, ROW_NUMBER never ties.

problems.title: Everyone under the CTO
problems.statement: List the `name` of everyone who reports to **Asha** (employee 1), directly or through other managers. Do not include Asha.
problems.expected: WITH RECURSIVE chain(id, name) AS (SELECT id, name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id) SELECT name FROM chain
problems.hint: Start with the direct reports, then repeatedly add people whose manager is already in the set (WITH RECURSIVE).
problems.note: A recursive CTE has an anchor query and a recursive step joined with UNION ALL; it stops when the step adds no rows.

problems.title: Hires per year
problems.statement: How many people were hired each year? Return `year` (as text, like `2020`) and `hires`, oldest year first.
problems.expected: SELECT strftime('%Y', hire_date) AS year, COUNT(*) AS hires FROM employees GROUP BY year ORDER BY year
problems.hint: strftime('%Y', hire_date) extracts the year in SQLite.
problems.note: Dates are stored as ISO text, so they sort and group correctly as strings.
